Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Gray ME
130 PM EST Fri Nov 6 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
No significant changes to overall forecast thinking this
afternoon...with rainfall totals 0.5-2.0 inches from northwest
to southeast.  

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1.Beneficial rainfall expands inland tonight with locally heavy 
rainfall along the coast with more showery conditions expected this 
weekend. 

2. Cooler temperatures arrive later this weekend and remain through
next week areawide. There will be multiple chances for light 
precipitation, including light snow or snow showers for the higher 
peaks of the White Mountains.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Band of shower/thunderstorm activity continues just south and 
east of a stalled frontal boundary along the coast of ME 
through southern New England. As impressive upstream closed low 
moves towards this boundary tonight...it will help back the 
low/mid level flow and push precipitation increasingly inland 
while at the same time low pressure will develop along the front
reaching a position within the Gulf of Maine by Saturday 
evening. Primary forecast concerns through Saturday night 
revolve around precipitation amounts...and then cooling 
temperatures by late Saturday/Saturday night as the upper low 
arrives from the west potentially changing the PTYPE to snow 
over the higher mountain peaks late Saturday night. 

QPF: Pretty sharp gradient from NW to SE given the frontal location. 
Have followed pretty close to REFS mean for totals through the 
period...with 0.5-0.75" in the mountains...around an inch in the 
foothills...and then 1.5-2" along the coastal plain.  While some 
poor drainage ponding is possible, especially given fallen
leaves...no widespread flooding is expected. 

Thunder:  Elevated instability has spawned a few lightning strikes 
north of the frontal boundary today across SE NH and far SW ME. This 
will likely continue through tonight with little overall motion to 
the frontal surface and modest mid level lapse rates ongoing.
This should end by daybreak Saturday as the warm sector pulls
further offshore.  

PTYPE:  Very warm to start the period with no PTYPE concerns.  As 
the upper low arrives Saturday night...thicknesses fall and we 
should see temperatures support a changeover to snow above 4kft by 
daybreak Sunday with some further cooling after that.  Thus...the 
highest peaks will see some accumulation before the low pulls away 
from the region. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
Sunday is expected to start out mostly cloudy with lingering 
light rain, but low pressure will exit to the east and northeast 
later in the day, with northwest winds in its wake pulling some 
drier air.  So we should see some peaks of sunshine in the 
afternoon, although the mountains and areas to the northwest will 
likely remain mostly cloudy with a chance of upslope showers, 
perhaps mixing with snow in the highest elevations. High 
temperatures will be in the 50s for most, except cooler in the 
40s in the mountains. 

Going into the first half of next week a more typical November 
pattern will be in place with longwave troughing across eastern 
Canada and into the Northeastern US. Shortwaves crossing through 
New England will bring multiple chances for light precipitation...
but primarily in the mountains with upslope flow in place. With
colder air aloft, expect some of this to be snow as we go up in
elevation, and some light accumulations will be possible on the
highest peaks. Elsewhere, periods of mostly cloudy skies are 
possible during the days with broad cyclonic flow in place, and 
precipitation chances are lower, but not zero, especially if 
Froude numbers are high enough. Highs will generally in the 50s 
except 40s across the north.

For the second half of the week, upslope mountain precip may 
continue in the mountains as troughing remains favored. Latest
ensemble also favors temperatures further trending cooler with 
highs perhaps limited to the 40s areawide. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z FRIDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...

Summary: Deteriorating conditions this evening as a wave of low 
pressure brings rain across most of the region.  Some improvement 
will occur on Saturday though showery conditions with some 
restrictions are expected through the weekend.  

Restrictions: Rain expands in coverage through this evening with 
conditions deteriorating to LIFR/IFR except LEB/HIE where 
restrictions will hold off until overnight as most of the rain 
passes south of these locations. Some minor improvement is expected 
Saturday morning though MVFR/IFR restrictions remain likely through 
the day with showers...with conditions likely deteriorating again 
Saturday night.  More substantial improvement is expected by the 
daytime on Sunday.  

Winds: Light/variable winds continue through this evening will 
gradually turn northerly /northeasterly along the coast/ 5-10kts 
overnight and remain northerly around 10kts for the day Saturday 
before diminishing to 5-10kts Saturday night.   

LLWS: LLWS is not expected through Saturday night.  

Thunder: Isolated thunderstorms possible all sites except
LEB/HIE through tonight. 

Outlook: An active pattern will bring low pressure across the region 
Monday and again Tuesday night with showers...esp in the mountains 
with MVFR restrictions likely at HIE and possibly LEB with other 
sites likely remaining mostly VFR with a few isolated restrictions 
as these low pressure areas move through. 

&&

.MARINE...
This evening through Saturday night: Winds remain light as a
frontal surface resides close to the Maine coast as of this
afternoon. Low pressure will develop along this front on 
Saturday...moving into the Gulf of Maine Saturday night. 
Northwest winds strengthen Saturday night...nearing SCA 
thresholds as we reach daybreak Sunday. 

Sunday-Friday...Low pressure lifts northward into the Maritimes 
Sunday into Monday and then remain in the vicinity of the Maritimes 
through at least the middle of next week. This will bring a general 
west to northwest over the waters, and periods of SCA conditions 
will be possible Sunday into early next week as multiple weak fronts 
cross. A weaker pressure gradient show allow winds and seas to 
remain below SCA levels for the second half of next week. 

&&
